section.title: oosqlGetAutocommit
section.para: Tests if a database connection is in autocommit mode.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
Returns true if the connection is in autocommit mode, and false if a transaction is in progress.

A connection is in autocommit mode by default: each statement is a transaction of its own. A BEGIN statement ends autocommit mode, and COMMIT or ROLLBACK restores it. After some errors inside a transaction, SQLite rolls it back automatically: this routine is the way to find out whether that happened.
The functionality of the oosqlGetAutocommit routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_get_autocommit API.
The getAutocommit method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.

This example shows the autocommit mode before, during, and after a transaction:
say oosqlGetAutocommit(db) -- 1 rc = oosqlExec(db, "BEGIN;") say oosqlGetAutocommit(db) -- 0 rc = oosqlExec(db, "UPDATE foods SET price = 2 WHERE id = 1;") rc = oosqlExec(db, "COMMIT;") say oosqlGetAutocommit(db) -- 1

section.title: oosqlInterrupt
section.para: Makes the SQL operations in progress on a database connection stop as soon as possible.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
Returns OK.

The interrupted operations return INTERRUPT. An INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE interrupted inside an explicit transaction rolls back the whole transaction. An operation that is about to finish may not be interrupted. Statements started while others are still running are interrupted too; when no statement is running, the routine has no effect.
The routine can be called from another thread, or from a callback routine, such as the one of oosqlProgressHandler. The connection must not be closed while oosqlInterrupt runs.
The functionality of the oosqlInterrupt routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_interrupt API.
The interrupt method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.

section.title: oosqlIsHandleNull
section.para: This routine provides a way for the programmer to check if a handle is null. The functions in ooSQLite that return handles will return a null handle on error. A null handle should never be used as an argument to any function.

listitem.para:
The single argument is:
handle
The handle to check.
Returns true if the handle is null, false if it is not null.
The oosqlBackupInit(), oosqlOpen(), oosqlPrepare() and several other functions return handles. These handles will be null on error.

If the programmer is not completely adverse to using object methods, the isNull() method can be invoked on a handle to test for null, rather than use the oosqlIsHandleNull() function. E.g
-- The following code snippet: if handle~isNull then ...
-- is equivalent to this snippet using the oosqlIsHandleNull() function: if oosqlIsHandleNull(handle) then ...
This function does not access any of the SQLite APIs. It is specific to ooSQLite.

This example opens a database connection and checks to be sure the returned handle is not null:
dbConn = oosqlOpen('contacts.rdbx') if oosqlIsHandleNull(dbConn) then do -- handle the error ... end

section.title: oosqlLastInsertRowID
section.para: Returns the rowid of the row inserted by the most recent successful INSERT on a database connection.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
The rowid, a 64-bit whole number, or 0 if no row has been inserted since the connection was opened.

Every row of a table has a rowid, which can be used in SQL with the names rowid, oid, or _rowid_. For a table with a column declared INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, that column is the rowid. A failed INSERT does not change the value; neither do the inserts made by triggers, once the statement that fired them is finished.
The functionality of the oosqlLastInsertRowID routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_last_insert_rowid API.
The lastInsertRowID method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.

This example inserts a row, and displays its rowid:
rc = oosqlExec(db, "INSERT INTO foods(type_id, name, price) VALUES(2, 'Ham', 4.5);") say 'The new row has rowid' oosqlLastInsertRowID(db) /* Output: The new row has rowid 5 */

section.title: oosqlLibVersion
section.para: Returns the version of the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses, as a string.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.
The version, such as 3.52.0.

The SQLite library is embedded in the ooSQLite library, so this is the version that the ooSQLite library was built with. The VERSION constant of the ooSQLiteConstants class has the version that ooSQLite.cls was written for: if they differ, ooSQLite.cls and the library do not belong together. Note that .ooSQLite~VERSION invokes the version method of the ooSQLite class, not the constant: use .ooSQLiteConstants~VERSION.
The functionality of the oosqlLibVersion routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_libversion API.
The libVersion method of the ooSQLite class does the same.

This example checks that ooSQLite.cls and the library match:
if oosqlLibVersion() \== .ooSQLiteConstants~VERSION then say 'ooSQLite.cls does not match the ooSQLite library' else say 'SQLite' oosqlLibVersion() /* Output might be: SQLite 3.52.0 */

section.title: oosqlLibVersionNumber
section.para: Returns the version of the SQLite library that ooSQLite uses, as a number.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.
The version as a whole number, X*1000000 + Y*1000 + Z for version X.Y.Z: 3052000 for version 3.52.0.
The number is easier to compare than the string that oosqlLibVersion returns. It is the same as the VERSION_NUMBER constant when ooSQLite.cls and the library match.
The functionality of the oosqlLibVersionNumber routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_libversion_number API.
The libVersionNumber method of the ooSQLite class does the same.

This example uses a feature of SQLite only if the library is recent enough:
if oosqlLibVersionNumber() < 3035000 then say 'RETURNING clauses need SQLite 3.35.0 or later' else do rows = oosqlExec(db, "DELETE FROM foods WHERE price IS NULL RETURNING name;", .true) say 'Deleted:' rows[1]['NAME'] end /* Output: Deleted: Cheese */

section.title: oosqlLimit
section.para: Queries or changes a run time limit of a database connection, such as the maximum length of an SQL statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
id [required]
The limit, one of the Run Time Limit constants, such as LIMIT_SQL_LENGTH.
value [required]
The new value of the limit. A negative value leaves the limit unchanged.
The value the limit had before the call. To query a limit without changing it, pass a negative value. For an id that is not one of the constants, -1 is returned.

Each limit has a maximum fixed when SQLite is compiled; a larger value is reduced to that maximum without error. Lowering the limits protects a program that executes SQL from sources that are not trusted.
The functionality of the oosqlLimit routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_limit API.
The limit method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object.

This example lowers the maximum length of an SQL statement, shows the error of a statement that is too long, and restores the limit:
say oosqlLimit(db, .ooSQLite~LIMIT_SQL_LENGTH, -1) -- 1000000000 old = oosqlLimit(db, .ooSQLite~LIMIT_SQL_LENGTH, 1000) say oosqlLimit(db, .ooSQLite~LIMIT_SQL_LENGTH, -1) -- 1000 say oosqlExec(db, "SELECT '"copies('x', 2000)"';") rc = oosqlLimit(db, .ooSQLite~LIMIT_SQL_LENGTH, old) /* Output: 1000000000 1000 SQLite Error: rc = 18, string or blob too big */

section.title: oosqlLoadExtension
section.para: Loads an SQLite extension library into a database connection.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
library [required]
The file name of the shared library. If SQLite can not load it with the name as given, it tries again adding the extension of the platform, such as .so or .dll.
entryPoint [optional]
The name of the initialization function of the library. If it is omitted, SQLite tries sqlite3_extension_init, and then a name derived from the file name of the library.
Returns OK on success, or ERROR on error: also when loading extensions has not been allowed with oosqlEnableLoadExtension.
Loading extensions must be allowed first with oosqlEnableLoadExtension. An extension stays loaded until the connection is closed.

The error message of SQLite, such as not authorized or the error of the operating system loader, is not recorded in the connection, so oosqlErrMsg does not return it. It is stored in the .local directory, with the index ROUTINEERRORMESSAGE, and can be retrieved as .routineErrorMessage. Each call to oosqlLoadExtension sets it to the empty string first. ooSQLiteRegisterBuiltin uses the same entry. Being in .local, it is shared by all the threads of the interpreter instance.
The functionality of the oosqlLoadExtension routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_load_extension API.
The extension libraries written for ooSQLite, with collations and functions in C, are loaded with the ooSQLExtensions class instead.

This example loads an extension library that defines the SQL function half, and uses it:
library = 'libsimpleextension.so' rc = oosqlEnableLoadExtension(db, .true) rc = oosqlLoadExtension(db, library) if rc == .ooSQLite~OK then do rows. = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT half(11) AS h;", .true) say 'half(11) =' rows.1['H'] end else say 'Error' rc':' .routineErrorMessage rc = oosqlEnableLoadExtension(db, .false) /* Output: half(11) = 5.5 */

section.title: oosqlMemoryHighWater
section.para: Returns the largest number of bytes of memory that SQLite has used at any one time.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
reset [optional]
If true, the mark is set to the memory in use, as oosqlMemoryUsed returns it, after its value is returned. The default is false.
The largest number of bytes in use at the same time since the process started, or since the mark was last reset. With reset, the value before the reset is returned.
Resetting the mark before an operation and reading it after tells how much memory the operation needed at its peak.
The functionality of the oosqlMemoryHighWater routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_memory_highwater API.
The memoryHighWater method of the ooSQLite class does the same.

This example measures the memory that a query needs. The numbers depend on the system and the version of SQLite:
call oosqlMemoryHighWater .true -- the mark is now the memory in use before = oosqlMemoryUsed() rows = oosqlExec(db, "WITH RECURSIVE c(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM c" - " WHERE i < 10000) SELECT max(randomblob(i % 1000)) FROM c ORDER BY 1;", .true) say 'In use before:' before say 'In use after: ' oosqlMemoryUsed() say 'Peak: ' oosqlMemoryHighWater() /* Output might be: In use before: 63688 In use after: 69016 Peak: 90784 */

section.title: oosqlMemoryUsed
section.para: Returns the number of bytes of memory that SQLite is using.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.
The number of bytes that SQLite has allocated and not freed yet, for all the connections of the process.
The memory used by the interpreter and by ooSQLite itself is not counted. oosqlMemoryHighWater returns the largest amount used.
The functionality of the oosqlMemoryUsed routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_memory_used API.
The memoryUsed method of the ooSQLite class does the same.
See the examples of oosqlMemoryHighWater and oosqlReleaseMemory.

section.title: &changed11;oosqlMutexAlloc
section.para: Allocates a new mutex, which the threads of a program can use to take turns.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
type [required]
The kind of mutex, one of the Mutex Type constants MUTEX_FAST or MUTEX_RECURSIVE. A thread that holds a recursive mutex can enter it again; a thread that holds a fast mutex must not.

A handle to the mutex, which is used with oosqlMutexEnter, oosqlMutexTry, oosqlMutexLeave, and oosqlMutexFree. The handle is null if SQLite was built without support for threads, see oosqlThreadSafe; the SQLite embedded in ooSQLite has that support.

What is said here applies to all the mutex routines. A mutex is held by one thread at a time: a thread enters it with oosqlMutexEnter, which waits while another thread holds it, or with oosqlMutexTry, which does not wait, and leaves it with oosqlMutexLeave. The thread that entered the mutex is the one that must leave it, once for each time it entered it. While a thread waits for a mutex, the other threads of the program keep running.

Breaking these rules has undefined results: entering a fast mutex again from the thread that holds it blocks the thread for ever, and leaving a mutex that the thread does not hold, or freeing it while it is held, can crash the interpreter. ooSQLite can not detect these. &changed11;A mutex that has been freed, and the mutex of a connection that has been closed, raise a syntax error, 88.900, in every mutex routine (see Handles); before ooSQLite 1.1 they could crash the interpreter too.

Every mutex allocated with oosqlMutexAlloc must be freed with oosqlMutexFree when it is no longer needed. In Rexx code, the guarded methods and the GUARD instruction of ooRexx also make threads take turns; an SQLite mutex is mostly useful when other code that uses SQLite takes part, or to hold the mutex of a connection, see oosqlDbMutex.
Raises a syntax error, 88.916, if type is not MUTEX_FAST or MUTEX_RECURSIVE. The other mutex types are the static mutexes that SQLite uses internally, and they can not be allocated.
The functionality of the oosqlMutexAlloc routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_mutex_alloc API.
The new method of the ooSQLiteMutex class creates a mutex object.

In this example, three threads add 1000 to a shared counter each. Each addition reads the counter, lets the other threads run, and writes it back, so without the mutex the threads would overwrite each other's work and the total would be much lower:
mtx = oosqlMutexAlloc(.ooSQLite~MUTEX_FAST) counter = .directory~new~~put(0, 'N') threads = .array~new do 3 threads~append(.message~new(.adder~new, 'add', 'I', mtx, counter)~~start) end do t over threads t~result -- waits until the thread ends end say counter['N'] call oosqlMutexFree mtx /* Output: 3000 */
::class adder ::method add use arg mtx, counter do 1000 call oosqlMutexEnter mtx n = counter['N'] call SysSleep 0 -- lets the other threads run counter['N'] = n + 1 call oosqlMutexLeave mtx end

section.title: oosqlMutexEnter
section.para: Enters a mutex, waiting until no other thread holds it.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
mtx [required]
The handle to a mutex, returned by oosqlMutexAlloc or by oosqlDbMutex. The handle must not be null, and the mutex must not have been freed.
Returns OK.

A recursive mutex can be entered again by the thread that holds it; a fast mutex must not. Each enter must be matched by an oosqlMutexLeave from the same thread. See the remarks of oosqlMutexAlloc for the rules that all the mutex routines follow.
Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if the handle is null.
The functionality of the oosqlMutexEnter routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_mutex_enter API.
The enter method of the ooSQLiteMutex class does the same for a mutex object.
See the examples of oosqlMutexAlloc and oosqlDbMutex.

section.title: &changed11;oosqlMutexFree
section.para: Frees a mutex allocated by oosqlMutexAlloc.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
mtx [required]
The handle to a mutex returned by oosqlMutexAlloc. The handle must not be null, and the mutex must not be held by any thread.
Returns OK.

After oosqlMutexFree, the handle is not valid any more: it must not be used in any routine, and it must not be freed again. The mutex of a connection, returned by oosqlDbMutex, belongs to SQLite and must never be freed. &changed11;In both cases oosqlMutexFree raises a syntax error, 88.900 (see Handles); before ooSQLite 1.1 it freed the memory again, or freed the mutex of the connection, and the process could abort or crash. See the remarks of oosqlMutexAlloc for the rules that all the mutex routines follow.
Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if the handle is null.
The functionality of the oosqlMutexFree routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_mutex_free API.
The free method of the ooSQLiteMutex class does the same for a mutex object.
See the examples of oosqlMutexAlloc and oosqlMutexTry.

section.title: oosqlMutexLeave
section.para: Leaves a mutex that the current thread holds.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
mtx [required]
The handle to a mutex, returned by oosqlMutexAlloc or by oosqlDbMutex. The handle must not be null, and the mutex must not have been freed.
Returns OK.

The mutex must have been entered by the same thread, with oosqlMutexEnter or with a successful oosqlMutexTry. A recursive mutex that was entered several times is released when it has been left as many times. See the remarks of oosqlMutexAlloc for the rules that all the mutex routines follow.
Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if the handle is null.
The functionality of the oosqlMutexLeave routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_mutex_leave API.
The leave method of the ooSQLiteMutex class does the same for a mutex object.
See the examples of oosqlMutexAlloc and oosqlDbMutex.

section.title: oosqlMutexTry
section.para: Tries to enter a mutex, without waiting if another thread holds it.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
mtx [required]
The handle to a mutex, returned by oosqlMutexAlloc or by oosqlDbMutex. The handle must not be null, and the mutex must not have been freed.
Returns OK if the mutex was entered: then it must be left with oosqlMutexLeave, as after oosqlMutexEnter. Returns BUSY if another thread holds the mutex.

A thread that holds a recursive mutex gets OK and enters it again. The result of trying a fast mutex that the same thread already holds is undefined. SQLite notes that on some systems this routine always returns BUSY, so a program should not depend on it to work. See the remarks of oosqlMutexAlloc for the rules that all the mutex routines follow.
Raises a syntax error, 88.900, if the handle is null.
The functionality of the oosqlMutexTry routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_mutex_try API.
The try method of the ooSQLiteMutex class does the same for a mutex object.

This example tries to enter a mutex from another thread, first while the main thread holds it, and then after it has left it:
mtx = oosqlMutexAlloc(.ooSQLite~MUTEX_FAST) call oosqlMutexEnter mtx say 'While this thread holds it:' tryInAnotherThread(mtx) call oosqlMutexLeave mtx say 'Once it has left it:' tryInAnotherThread(mtx) call oosqlMutexFree mtx /* Output: While this thread holds it: busy Once it has left it: entered */
::routine tryInAnotherThread use arg mtx return .message~new(.tryer~new, 'try', 'I', mtx)~~start~result
::class tryer ::method try use arg mtx if oosqlMutexTry(mtx) == .ooSQLite~BUSY then return 'busy' call oosqlMutexLeave mtx return 'entered'

section.title: &changed11;oosqlNextStmt
section.para: Finds the prepared statements of a database connection, one by one.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null, and the connection must not have been closed: see oosqlClose.
stmt [optional]
The handle to a statement of the connection. If it is omitted, or is .nil, the first statement is found.
The handle to the statement that follows stmt, or to the first statement, or .nil if there is none.

The statements are found in no particular order: the most recently prepared one usually comes first. stmt must not have been finalized: to finalize all the statements of a connection, find the next statement before finalizing the current one, as the example does. &changed11;A statement that has been finalized, or that belongs to another connection, raises a syntax error, 88.900 (see Handles); before ooSQLite 1.1 the first could crash the interpreter, and the second went on with the statements of the other connection.
Raises a syntax error if stmt is neither a Pointer object nor .nil.
The functionality of the oosqlNextStmt routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_next_stmt API.
The nextStmt method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same for a connection object, with ooSQLiteStmt objects.

This example finalizes all the statements of a connection, and then closes it:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT name FROM foods;", 'stmt1') rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT price FROM foods;", 'stmt2')
stmt = oosqlNextStmt(db) do while stmt \== .nil next = oosqlNextStmt(db, stmt) -- before stmt is finalized say 'Finalizing:' oosqlSql(stmt) call oosqlFinalize stmt stmt = next end say oosqlClose(db) /* Output: Finalizing: SELECT price FROM foods; Finalizing: SELECT name FROM foods; 0 */

section.title: &changed11;oosqlOpen
section.para: Opens a database connection.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
dbFileName [required]
The file name of the database to open. The special string :memory: can be used to open an in memory database. The dbFileName argument can also be an URI. Refer to the SQLite documentation for details.
dbConn [required]
The string name of a variable in the Rexx program that will be set to the handle to the database connection. Note that this is the string name of the variable, not the variable itself. The variable may, but does not need to, already exist in the program.
openFlags [optional]
One or more of the file open constants. This flag controls how the database is opened. Do not use any constant marked as VFS only. Use ooSQLiteMerge() to merge two or more of the constant values to together, if needed.
The 3 common flags are OPEN_READWRITE, OPEN_READONLY, and OPEN_CREATE. If this argument is omitted, the OPEN_READWRITE merged with OPEN_CREATE flags are used.
reserved [optional]
This argument is reserved for future enhancement. It is completely ignored in the current implementation.
Returns one of the SQLite result codes. OK on success, otherwise an error code.
When the function returns, the variable named by the dbConn argument will always be set to a handle to the database connection. This is true even if the return code indicates and error.

On success, the database connection handle can be used as an argument in any other function that requires a database connection handle. To prevent resource leaks, oosqlClose must be called on each database connection returned by oosqlOpen. This is true even if oosqlOpen returns an error. &changed11;Once oosqlClose has returned OK, the handle is not valid any more, and the routines raise a syntax error, 88.900, when they are given it: see Handles.

On error, the handle can be used in the oosqlErrMsg function to obtain a description of the error. It can also be used in the oosqlErrCode function, although at this point the return from oosqlErrCode will be the same as the return code from oosqlOpen. There is one exception to this. If the error return is NOMEM the handle will be null. Do not use a null handle in any other function.

The oosqlIsHandleNull() function can be used to test for a null handle. However testing for a return of NOMEM is sufficient. The handle will always be null when the return is NOMEM and not null for any other return.

The openFlags argument is the binary or value of the individual open constants. If the programmer is comfortable with the binary or operation, that can be used instead of the ooSQLiteMerge() function.
The functionality of the oosqlOpen() routine is similar to that of the sqlite3_open_v2 SQLite API

This example opens the ooFoods.rdbx database and checks for any errors:
ret = oosqlOpen('ooFoods.rdbx', 'db') if ret == .ooSQLite~NOMEM then do say 'Unrecoverable error, quitting.' return 99 end
if oosqlErrCode(db) <> .ooSQLite~OK then do -- handle the error .. oosqlClose(db) ... end
-- We have a good connection, use the database. ...

section.title: oosqlPrepare
section.para: Prepares a SQL statement to be executed by the database engine. To execute a SQL statement, SQLite first compiles the statement into a byte-code program. This can be thought of as preparing, or initializing the statement.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to an open database connection. The handle can not be null and the connection can not have been closed.
sql [required]
The SQL statement to prepare.
_stmt [required]
The string name of a variable in the Rexx program that will be set to the handle to the prepared statement. Note that this is the string name of the variable, not the variable itself. The variable may, but does not need to, already exist in the program.
_tail [optional]
The string name of a variable in the Rexx program that will be set to the value of the tail to the prepared statement. Note that this is the string name of the variable, not the variable itself. The variable may, but does not need to, already exist in the program.
SQLite only compiles the first SQL statement in sql, that is, up to the first semicolon that ends a statement. If _tail is not omitted, and the statement is prepared without error, the variable named by _tail is set to the text that follows the first statement. This may of course be the empty string. The example of oosqlSql uses it to execute several statements, one by one.
Returns OK on success, or one of the Result Code constants on error. oosqlErrMsg describes the error.

The variable named by the _stmt argument will always be set on return from this function call. On success this will be a handle to a prepared statement which can be used in any function requiring a prepared statement. On an error return this handle will always be null. Never use a null handle in any function.

Each successful call to oosqlPrepare must be matched with a call to oosqlFinalize to prevent resource leaks. oosqlFinalize can be called at any time after oosqlPrepare. Normally it would be called when the program is done with the prepared statement. Note that oosqlFinalize is one exception to never use a null handle in a function call. It is a harmless no-op to call oosqlFinalize with a null handle.
Never use the prepared statement after it has been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.
Note that if the sql argument is the empty string, or contains only blanks or comments, the return code is OK, but the handle to the prepared statement is null: there is no statement to execute.
The functionality of the oosqlPrepare() routine is similar to that of the sqlite3_prepare_v2 SQLite API.

This example prepares a query, displays its result rows, and finalizes the statement:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT id, name FROM foods WHERE type_id = 1 ORDER BY name;", 'stmt') if rc <> .ooSQLite~OK then do say 'Error preparing the statement:' oosqlErrMsg(db) return rc end do while oosqlStep(stmt) == .ooSQLite~ROW say oosqlColumnInt(stmt, 1)~right(4) oosqlColumnText(stmt, 2) end call oosqlFinalize stmt /* Output: 1 Bagels 2 Bagels, raisin */

section.title: oosqlProfile
section.para: Registers a routine that is called with the text of each SQL statement, and the time it took, when it finishes executing.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
rtnName [required]
The name of the public routine to call for each statement, or the empty string to remove the routine registered before. See the rules for callback routines.
userData [optional]
Any object, passed to the routine as its third argument. If it is omitted, the routine receives .nil.
Returns the userData of the routine that was registered before, or .nil if there was none, or it had no user data.

The routine is called with three arguments: the SQL text, the time the statement took, in nanoseconds, and the user data. The time is wall clock time, and its resolution is only of milliseconds on most systems. The routine must return a whole number, which is ignored.
A connection has only one of profile and trace routine: registering one removes the other.
The functionality of the oosqlProfile routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_profile API.
The profile method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same with a method of an object; see also profileCallBack.

This example displays the time each statement takes:
rc = oosqlProfile(db, 'showTime') rc = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT count(*) FROM foods; UPDATE foods SET price = 3 WHERE id = 1;") rc = oosqlProfile(db, '') /* Output might be: 0 ms SELECT count(*) FROM foods; 2 ms UPDATE foods SET price = 3 WHERE id = 1; */
::routine showTime public use arg sql, nanoseconds say (nanoseconds % 1000000)~right(4) 'ms ' sql return 0

section.title: oosqlProgressHandler
section.para: Registers a routine that is called periodically while SQL is executed, and that can interrupt it.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
rtnName [required]
The name of the public routine to call periodically, or the empty string to remove the routine registered before. See the rules for callback routines.
instructions [required]
The number of virtual machine instructions SQLite executes between two calls of the routine. If it is 0 or less, the routine is not called.
userData [optional]
Any object, passed to the routine as its only argument. If it is omitted, the routine receives .nil.
Returns OK.

The routine is called with one argument, the user data. It must return a whole number: 0 to let the operation go on, or any other value to interrupt it, and then the statement returns INTERRUPT. A program can use it to show that it is working, or to cancel a query that takes too long.
The routine must not use the connection: it must not prepare or execute SQL on it.
The functionality of the oosqlProgressHandler routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_progress_handler API.
The progressHandler method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same with a method of an object; see also progressCallBack.

This example stops a query that would never end, after the routine has been called 10 times:
calls = .directory~new calls~count = 0 rc = oosqlProgressHandler(db, 'stopAfter10', 1000, calls) sql = "WITH RECURSIVE c(x) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT x + 1 FROM c) SELECT count(*) FROM c;" say oosqlExec(db, sql) say calls~count 'call(s)' rc = oosqlProgressHandler(db, '', 0) /* Output: SQLite Error: rc = 9, interrupted 10 call(s) */
::routine stopAfter10 public use arg calls calls~count += 1 return calls~count >= 10 -- 1 stops the query

section.title: oosqlReleaseMemory
section.para: Asks SQLite to free memory that it does not need, such as the pages of the databases that it keeps in its cache.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
nBytes [required]
The number of bytes to free.
The number of bytes that were freed, which can be more or less than nBytes.

The memory freed is mostly that of the page cache of the connections, which SQLite fills again when it needs the pages. The pages of an in-memory database are the database itself, and are never freed. oosqlDbReleaseMemory frees the memory of a single connection.
The functionality of the oosqlReleaseMemory routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_release_memory API.
The releaseMemory method of the ooSQLite class does the same.

This example fills the cache with the pages of a new table, and then frees part of it. The numbers depend on the system and the version of SQLite:
rc = oosqlExec(db, "CREATE TABLE notes(text); WITH RECURSIVE c(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL" - " SELECT i + 1 FROM c WHERE i < 5000) INSERT INTO notes SELECT hex(randomblob(200)) FROM c;") rows = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT count(*) FROM notes;", .true) -- the pages are in the cache now say 'In use: ' oosqlMemoryUsed() say 'Released:' oosqlReleaseMemory(1000000) say 'In use: ' oosqlMemoryUsed() /* Output might be: In use: 2176360 Released: 1000272 In use: 1176088 */

section.title: oosqlReset
section.para: Resets a prepared statement to its initial state, so that it can be executed again.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
stmt [required]
The handle to a statement prepared by oosqlPrepare. The handle must not be null, and the statement must not have been finalized: see the rules for statement handles.

Returns OK if the last execution of the statement had no error, or if it was never executed. If the last oosqlStep failed, the error code it returned is returned again. In both cases, the statement is reset.

A statement can be reset at any time, whether it has been run to completion or not. Resetting a statement does not change the values bound to its parameters: use oosqlClearBindings for that. After a reset, new values can be bound, and the statement is executed again by stepping it. Reusing a statement in this way is faster than preparing a new one.
The functionality of the oosqlReset routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_reset API.
The reset method of the ooSQLiteStmt class does the same for a statement object.

This example executes the same query for three different values of its parameter:
rc = oosqlPrepare(db, "SELECT count(*) FROM foods WHERE type_id = ?;", 'stmt') do type = 1 to 3 rc = oosqlBindInt(stmt, 1, type) rc = oosqlStep(stmt) say 'type' type':' oosqlColumnInt(stmt, 1) 'food(s)' rc = oosqlReset(stmt) end call oosqlFinalize stmt /* Output: type 1: 2 food(s) type 2: 1 food(s) type 3: 1 food(s) */

section.title: oosqlResetAutoExtension
section.para: Removes all the extensions from the list of automatic extensions.

listitem.para: There are no arguments.
Returns OK.

The list belongs to the process, so the extensions made automatic by any part of the program, also with the autoBuiltin method of the ooSQLExtensions class, are removed. The connections where they were already registered keep them. See the remarks of oosqlAutoExtension for how automatic extensions work.
The functionality of the oosqlResetAutoExtension routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_reset_auto_extension API.
The resetAutoBuiltin method of the ooSQLExtensions class does the same.

This example makes two extensions automatic, and removes them both:
call oosqlAutoExtension 'rot13' call oosqlAutoExtension 'base64' say 'Reset:' oosqlResetAutoExtension() rc = oosqlOpen(':memory:', 'other') say oosqlPrepare(other, "SELECT base64('abc');", 'stmt') oosqlErrMsg(other) call oosqlClose other /* Output: Reset: 0 1 no such function: base64 */

section.title: &changed11;oosqlResultBlob
section.para: Sets the result of a user defined SQL function, or of the final step of an aggregate, to a blob. It is used inside the callback routines registered with oosqlCreateFunction. This is the classic interface equivalent of the blob method of the ooSQLResult class.

listitem.para: The arguments are:
The SQLite context, the second argument of the callback routine.

The data of the blob: a String, a Buffer, or a MutableBuffer object, as for oosqlBindBlob, such as the one returned by oosqlValueBlob, or a Pointer object to the data. Before ooSQLite 1.1 only a Pointer was accepted.

varlistentry.term: &changed11;size [optional with a String, Buffer, or MutableBuffer, required with a Pointer]

listitem.para: The number of bytes of the blob. With a String, a Buffer, or a MutableBuffer, the blob is made of the first size bytes of the data, which must be from 0 to the length of the data; if it is omitted, all the data is used. With a Pointer it is the number of bytes to copy from that address.
Returns 0. SQLite copies the data, so it can be discarded after the call.

What is said here applies to all the oosqlResult routines. They set the value that a user defined SQL function returns to the statement that invoked it, and they are used inside the routines registered with oosqlCreateFunction: the routine of a function, and the final routine of an aggregate. The sqlCntxt is the second argument of that routine, a Pointer object that is only valid during that invocation of the routine.

The routine can set the result more than once: the last value set is the one returned. If it sets no result, the function returns NULL. The routines that set an error, such as oosqlResultError, make the statement that invoked the function fail.
The functionality of the oosqlResultBlob routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_result_blob API.
This example defines a SQL function, fromHex, that turns a hexadecimal string into a blob:
listitem.programlisting:
call oosqlOpen ":memory:", "db" call oosqlCreateFunction db, "fromHex", 1, "fromHexRtn" rows = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT hex(fromHex('CAFE')) AS h;", .true, .ooSQLite~OO_ARRAY_OF_DIRECTORIES) say rows[1]["H"] -- CAFE call oosqlClose db
::requires "ooSQLite.cls"
::routine fromHexRtn public use arg db, context, userData, value call oosqlResultBlob context, oosqlValueText(value)~x2c return 0

section.title: oosqlResultDouble
section.para: Sets the result of a user defined SQL function, or of the final step of an aggregate, to a floating point number.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
sqlCntxt [required]
The SQLite context, the second argument of the function routine, or of the final routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob.
value [required]
The number. It is converted to a double precision floating point number.
Returns 0.
See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob for when and how the result is set.
Raises a syntax error if value is not a number.
The functionality of the oosqlResultDouble routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_result_double API.
The double method of the ooSQLResult class does the same in the object orientated interface.

This example defines a withTax function that adds a 21 percent tax to a price. A NULL price gives a NULL result:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "withTax", 1, "withTaxRtn") sql = "SELECT name, quote(withTax(price)) AS p FROM foods;" rows = oosqlExec(db, sql, .true, .ooSQLite~OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS) do i = 2 to rows~items say rows[i][1]':' rows[i][2] end /* Output: Bagels: 1.5125 Bagels, raisin: 1.815 Bacon: 4.5375 Cheese: NULL */
::routine withTaxRtn public use arg db, context, userData, price if oosqlValueType(price) == .ooSQLite~SQLNULL then call oosqlResultNull context else call oosqlResultDouble context, oosqlValueDouble(price) * 1.21 return 0

section.title: oosqlResultError
section.para: Makes a user defined SQL function, or the final step of an aggregate, fail with an error message.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
sqlCntxt [required]
The SQLite context, the second argument of the function routine, or of the final routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob.
errMsg [required]
The text of the error message.
Returns 0.

The statement that invoked the function fails: oosqlStep returns ERROR, and oosqlErrMsg returns errMsg. oosqlResultErrorCode sets another error code; when it is invoked after oosqlResultError, the message is kept. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob for when and how the result is set.
The functionality of the oosqlResultError routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_result_error API.
The error method of the ooSQLResult class does the same in the object orientated interface.

This example defines a checkPrice function that fails when a food has no price:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "checkPrice", 2, "checkPriceRtn") say oosqlExec(db, "SELECT checkPrice(name, price) FROM foods;") say oosqlErrCode(db) oosqlErrMsg(db) /* Output: SQLite Error: rc = 1, Cheese has no price 1 Cheese has no price */
::routine checkPriceRtn public use arg db, context, userData, name, price if oosqlValueType(price) == .ooSQLite~SQLNULL then do call oosqlResultError context, oosqlValueText(name) 'has no price' return 0 end call oosqlResultValue context, price return 0

section.title: oosqlResultErrorCode
section.para: Makes a user defined SQL function, or the final step of an aggregate, fail with an error code.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
sqlCntxt [required]
The SQLite context, the second argument of the function routine, or of the final routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob.
errCode [required]
The error code, one of the Result Code constants, such as CONSTRAINT.
Returns 0.

The statement that invoked the function fails with errCode. The error message is the one set by oosqlResultError, if it was invoked before; otherwise, it is the standard message for the code, the one that oosqlErrStr returns. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob for when and how the result is set.
The functionality of the oosqlResultErrorCode routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_result_error_code API.
The errorCode method of the ooSQLResult class does the same in the object orientated interface.

This example makes a function fail with the code CONSTRAINT and its own message:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "costly", 1, "costlyRtn") say oosqlExec(db, "SELECT costly(price) FROM foods;") say oosqlErrCode(db) oosqlErrMsg(db) /* Output: SQLite Error: rc = 19, Bacon is too expensive 19 Bacon is too expensive */
::routine costlyRtn public use arg db, context, userData, price if oosqlValueDouble(price) > 3 then do call oosqlResultError context, 'Bacon is too expensive' call oosqlResultErrorCode context, .ooSQLite~CONSTRAINT end else call oosqlResultValue context, price return 0

section.title: oosqlResultErrorNoMem
section.para: Makes a user defined SQL function, or the final step of an aggregate, fail because it ran out of memory.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlCntxt [required]
The SQLite context, the second argument of the function routine, or of the final routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob.
Returns 0.
The statement that invoked the function fails with the code NOMEM and the message out of memory. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob for when and how the result is set.
The functionality of the oosqlResultErrorNoMem routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_result_error_nomem API.
The errorNoMem method of the ooSQLResult class does the same in the object orientated interface.
See the example of oosqlResultErrorTooBig, which works in the same way.

section.title: oosqlResultErrorTooBig
section.para: Makes a user defined SQL function, or the final step of an aggregate, fail because a string or a blob is too big.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlCntxt [required]
The SQLite context, the second argument of the function routine, or of the final routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob.
Returns 0.
The statement that invoked the function fails with the code TOOBIG and the message string or blob too big. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob for when and how the result is set.
The functionality of the oosqlResultErrorTooBig routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_result_error_toobig API.
The errorTooBig method of the ooSQLResult class does the same in the object orientated interface.

This example defines a shortName function that does not accept names longer than 10 characters:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "shortName", 1, "shortNameRtn") say oosqlExec(db, "SELECT shortName(name) FROM foods;") /* Output: SQLite Error: rc = 18, string or blob too big */
::routine shortNameRtn public use arg db, context, userData, name text = oosqlValueText(name) if length(text) > 10 then call oosqlResultErrorTooBig context else call oosqlResultText context, text return 0

section.title: oosqlResultInt
section.para: Sets the result of a user defined SQL function, or of the final step of an aggregate, to a 32-bit integer.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
sqlCntxt [required]
The SQLite context, the second argument of the function routine, or of the final routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob.
value [required]
The whole number, which must fit in 32 bits: from -2147483648 to 2147483647. Use oosqlResultInt64 for larger numbers.
Returns 0.
See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob for when and how the result is set.
Raises a syntax error if value is not a whole number that fits in 32 bits.
The functionality of the oosqlResultInt routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_result_int API.
The int method of the ooSQLResult class does the same in the object orientated interface.

This example defines a words function that counts the words of a text, and uses it in a WHERE clause:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "words", 1, "wordsRtn") sql = "SELECT name, words(name) AS w FROM foods WHERE words(name) > 1;" rows = oosqlExec(db, sql, .true, .ooSQLite~OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS) say rows[2][1]':' rows[2][2] 'words' /* Output: Bagels, raisin: 2 words */
::routine wordsRtn public use arg db, context, userData, text call oosqlResultInt context, words(oosqlValueText(text)) return 0

section.title: oosqlResultInt64
section.para: Sets the result of a user defined SQL function, or of the final step of an aggregate, to a 64-bit integer.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
sqlCntxt [required]
The SQLite context, the second argument of the function routine, or of the final routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob.
value [required]
The whole number, which must fit in 64 bits: from -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807.
Returns 0.

The routine that computes the value may need a higher NUMERIC DIGITS setting than the default of 9, as the example does. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob for when and how the result is set. The example of oosqlValueInt64 also uses oosqlResultInt64.
Raises a syntax error if value is not a whole number that fits in 64 bits.
The functionality of the oosqlResultInt64 routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_result_int64 API.
The int64 method of the ooSQLResult class does the same in the object orientated interface.

This example defines a factorial function. The factorial of 20 does not fit in 32 bits:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "factorial", 1, "factorialRtn") sql = "SELECT factorial(20) AS f, typeof(factorial(20)) AS t;" rows = oosqlExec(db, sql, .true, .ooSQLite~OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS) say rows[2][1] rows[2][2] /* Output: 2432902008176640000 integer */
::routine factorialRtn public use arg db, context, userData, n numeric digits 20 f = 1 do i = 2 to oosqlValueInt(n) f = f * i end call oosqlResultInt64 context, f return 0

section.title: oosqlResultNull
section.para: Sets the result of a user defined SQL function, or of the final step of an aggregate, to NULL.

listitem.para:
The only argument is:
sqlCntxt [required]
The SQLite context, the second argument of the function routine, or of the final routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob.
Returns 0.
A function whose routine sets no result also returns NULL, but setting it explicitly makes the intent clear. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob for when and how the result is set.
The functionality of the oosqlResultNull routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_result_null API.
The null method of the ooSQLResult class does the same in the object orientated interface.
See the examples of oosqlResultDouble and oosqlResultValue.

section.title: oosqlResultText
section.para: Sets the result of a user defined SQL function, or of the final step of an aggregate, to a text.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
sqlCntxt [required]
The SQLite context, the second argument of the function routine, or of the final routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob.
txt [required]
The string. SQLite expects the text to be UTF-8. The text ends at its first NUL character, if it has one: use oosqlResultBlob for data that can contain NUL characters.
Returns 0.
SQLite copies the text. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob for when and how the result is set.
The functionality of the oosqlResultText routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_result_text API.
The text method of the ooSQLResult class does the same in the object orientated interface.

This example defines an initials function that returns the first letter of each word of a name:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "initials", 1, "initialsRtn") sql = "SELECT name, initials(name) AS i FROM foods;" rows = oosqlExec(db, sql, .true, .ooSQLite~OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS) do i = 2 to rows~items say rows[i][1]':' rows[i][2] end /* Output: Bagels: B Bagels, raisin: BR Bacon: B Cheese: C */
::routine initialsRtn public use arg db, context, userData, name text = oosqlValueText(name) initials = '' do i = 1 to words(text) initials ||= left(word(text, i), 1)~upper end call oosqlResultText context, initials return 0

section.title: &changed11;oosqlResultValue
section.para: Sets the result of a user defined SQL function, or of the final step of an aggregate, to a copy of one of the values passed to the function. The result keeps the datatype of the value.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
sqlCntxt [required]
The SQLite context, the second argument of the function routine, or of the final routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob.
value [required]
One of the values that SQLite passes to the routine: the fourth and following arguments of the routine of a function, or the fifth and following arguments of the step routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlValueBlob.
Returns 0.

The value must be one of the values passed to the current invocation of the routine, or a value returned by oosqlColumnValue while its statement stays on the same result row. &changed11;Any other Pointer raises a syntax error, 88.900, and so does a value passed to an invocation that has ended, or a value whose statement has been finalized (see Handles). Before ooSQLite 1.1 they could crash the interpreter. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob for when and how the result is set.
Raises a syntax error if value is not a Pointer object.
The functionality of the oosqlResultValue routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_result_value API.
The value method of the ooSQLResult class does the same in the object orientated interface.

This example defines a firstOf function, with any number of arguments, that returns the first one that is not NULL. The result keeps its type:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "firstOf", -1, "firstOfRtn") sql = "SELECT name, firstOf(price, type_id, 'none') AS v," - "typeof(firstOf(price, type_id, 'none')) AS t FROM foods WHERE id > 2;" rows = oosqlExec(db, sql, .true, .ooSQLite~OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS) do i = 2 to rows~items say rows[i][1]':' rows[i][2] '('rows[i][3]')' end /* Output: Bacon: 3.75 (real) Cheese: 3 (integer) */
::routine firstOfRtn public use arg db, context, userData, ... do i = 4 to arg() if oosqlValueType(arg(i)) \== .ooSQLite~SQLNULL then do call oosqlResultValue context, arg(i) return 0 end end call oosqlResultNull context return 0

section.title: oosqlResultZeroBlob
section.para: Sets the result of a user defined SQL function, or of the final step of an aggregate, to a blob filled with zeros.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
sqlCntxt [required]
The SQLite context, the second argument of the function routine, or of the final routine of an aggregate. See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob.
size [required]
The size of the blob, in bytes. A negative size is the same as 0.
Returns 0.
See the remarks of oosqlResultBlob for when and how the result is set.
The functionality of the oosqlResultZeroBlob routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_result_zeroblob API.
The zeroBlob method of the ooSQLResult class does the same in the object orientated interface.

This example defines a blank function, and uses it to set the picture of a food to 8 zero bytes:
rc = oosqlCreateFunction(db, "blank", 1, "blankRtn") rc = oosqlExec(db, "UPDATE foods SET picture = blank(8) WHERE id = 1;") sql = "SELECT length(picture) AS l, hex(picture) AS h FROM foods WHERE id =" - "1;" rows = oosqlExec(db, sql, .true, .ooSQLite~OO_ARRAY_OF_ARRAYS) say rows[2][1] rows[2][2] /* Output: 8 0000000000000000 */
::routine blankRtn public use arg db, context, userData, size call oosqlResultZeroBlob context, oosqlValueInt(size) return 0

section.title: oosqlRollbackHook
section.para: Registers a routine that is called whenever a transaction is rolled back.

listitem.para:
The arguments are:
db [required]
The handle to a database connection, as set by oosqlOpen. The handle must not be null.
rtnName [required]
The name of the public routine to call after each rollback, or the empty string to remove the routine registered before. See the rules for callback routines.
userData [optional]
Any object, passed to the routine as its only argument. If it is omitted, the routine receives .nil.
Returns the userData of the routine that was registered before, or .nil if there was none, or it had no user data.

The routine is called with one argument, the user data. It must return a whole number, which is ignored. It is called for an explicit ROLLBACK, for a COMMIT that the commit hook turns into a rollback, and for the rollbacks caused by errors; it is not called when the connection is closed with a transaction open.
The routine must not use the connection: it must not prepare or execute SQL on it.
The functionality of the oosqlRollbackHook routine is similar to that of the SQLite sqlite3_rollback_hook API.
The rollbackHook method of the ooSQLiteConnection class does the same with a method of an object; see also rollbackHookCallBack.

This example registers a commit hook that refuses every commit, and a rollback hook that reports it:
rc = oosqlCommitHook(db, 'refuseCommit') rc = oosqlRollbackHook(db, 'onRollback') say oosqlExec(db, "DELETE FROM foods;") rows. = oosqlExec(db, "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM foods;", .true) say rows.1['N'] 'food(s) left' rc = oosqlCommitHook(db, '') rc = oosqlRollbackHook(db, '') /* Output: Rolled back SQLite Error: rc = 531, constraint failed 4 food(s) left */
::routine refuseCommit public return 1 -- turn every COMMIT into a ROLLBACK
::routine onRollback public say 'Rolled back' return 0
